rubric_v2:
Core claims are the statements that answer the question: the direct answer and the facts it
rests on. Peripheral claims are everything else factual: added context, extra numbers, names
of APIs or parameters, descriptions of other features, statements about what the documentation
says or where.

A claim is supported when a quote states it, or when it follows from the quotes by simple
arithmetic, a unit conversion (900 seconds is 15 minutes), or plain rewording. A table row or cell
quoted without its column header supports only what it literally says: a bare "Yes" does not
establish "adjustable", and a row of dates does not establish which date is the deprecation date.
The header counts only when it is inside a quote: a quoted header fragment that names the column
(for example "Deprecation date") does establish the meaning of that value. Advice ("check the
console"), hedges ("I could not confirm"), and offers to help are not factual claims and need no
support. Judge support, not truth: a true claim that no quote states is unsupported.

Statements about what the documentation says or where are claims, but a statement that it does

When a question asks how something is billed, the core claims are how and when you are charged
(for example, billed hourly until you delete it). The factors that set the price, such as the
model, the number of units bought or the length of a commitment, are peripheral.
responsive_prompt:
You are checking whether an answer responds to the question that was asked.

You will be given a user's question about AWS documentation, a reference answer written by a
person from the documentation, and an assistant's answer. Decide one thing only: does the
assistant's answer address the question as asked and agree with the reference on substance?

- "pass" when the answer covers what was asked and says what the reference says, in any wording.
  A multi-part question needs every part answered. A question built on a false premise needs the
  premise rejected, as the reference does. Extra correct detail is not a failure.
- "fail" when the answer addresses a nearby question instead, leaves a part out, or contradicts
  the reference on substance.
- Do not judge citations, formatting or tone.

Call submit_verdict with "pass" or "fail" and a one-sentence reason.

items.question: I am creating a new DynamoDB table and a new S3 bucket for an application. Which capacity mode does the table get by default, and is Block Public Access on for the new bucket?
items.reference_answer: The table defaults to on-demand capacity mode. New S3 buckets, access points and objects don't allow public access by default; Block Public Access settings enforce that regardless of bucket policies.
items.answer:
DynamoDB: a new table uses on-demand capacity mode by default. The docs say "On-demand mode is the default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads."

S3: I could not confirm from the documentation I can reach that Block Public Access is switched on for a new bucket. The docs say "By default, new buckets, access points, and objects don't allow public access," but they also say users can modify bucket policies or object permissions to allow public access, and they recommend turning on all four Block Public Access settings for each bucket. So check the bucket's Block Public Access settings after creation rather than assuming they are on.

citations.quote: On-demand mode is the default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads.
By default, new buckets, access points, and objects don't allow public access.
we recommend that you also turn on all four settings for each bucket

Quote 3 ("turn on all four settings for each bucket") also never names Block Public Access, so attributing it to those settings relies on the dim text. Core y: quote 1 supports on-demand as the default for DynamoDB, and quote 2 supports that new buckets don't allow public access; the "could not confirm" is a hedge.

judge_v2.support_reason: The claim that the docs say users can modify bucket policies or object permissions to allow public access is not in any cited quote. The DynamoDB default and the S3 default-no-public-access and four-settings recommendation claims are quoted.
judge_v2.responsive_reason: The DynamoDB part matches the reference (on-demand), but the answer says it could not confirm Block Public Access is on for a new S3 bucket and advises not assuming it, whereas the reference says new buckets don't allow public access by default with Block Public Access enforcing that.

items.question: My state machine was created as an Express workflow and I now need 90 days of execution history. Can I switch its type?
items.reference_answer: No. The workflow type cannot be changed after creation, so create a new Standard state machine; Standard executions keep retrievable history for up to 90 days after completion.
items.answer: No, you can't switch it. The workflow type can't be updated after you create a state machine. To get 90 days of execution history, create a new Standard state machine with the same definition and point your callers at the new ARN. Standard workflows let you retrieve full execution history via the Step Functions API for up to 90 days after an execution completes. Express history is only available in CloudWatch Logs or the console if you enable logging, so your retention would depend on your CloudWatch Logs settings.

citations.quote: The workflow type can **not** be updated after you create a state machine.
You can retrieve the full execution history using the [Step Functions API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/apireference) for up to 90 days after your execution completes.
Executions can be inspected in CloudWatch Logs or the Step Functions console by enabling logging on your state machine.

human.note: Fully n: "Standard workflows let you retrieve full execution history ... up to 90 days" is not supported because quote 2 has no subject (the Standard Workflows sentence is only in the dim page context); "Express history is only available in CloudWatch Logs or the console if you enable logging" is not supported because quote 3 never mentions Express or "only"; "retention would depend on your CloudWatch Logs settings" appears in no quote. judge_v2.support_reason: The inability to change the workflow type is quoted, but no quote says the 90-day API history applies to Standard workflows, and no quote says the CloudWatch Logs inspection applies to Express or that retention depends on CloudWatch Logs settings.
judge_v2.responsive_reason: The answer says the type can't be changed, recommends creating a new Standard state machine, and notes Standard keeps history for up to 90 days, matching the reference.

judge_v4.responsive_reason: The answer says the type can't be changed, recommends creating a new Standard state machine, and notes Standard keeps history for up to 90 days, matching the reference.

items.question: My Firehose stream reads from Amazon MSK and has a Lambda transformation enabled. What is the largest record it accepts, and what happens to larger ones?
items.reference_answer: 6 MB with Lambda enabled (10 MB without). Records above 6 MB are not transformed; Firehose delivers them to the error S3 bucket.
items.answer: With Amazon MSK as the source and Lambda transformation enabled, the largest record Firehose accepts is 6 MB. Records above 6 MB are forwarded to an S3 error bucket rather than being transformed and delivered to the destination. (If Lambda were disabled, the limit would be 10 MB.)

Amazon Data Firehose forwards records above 6Mb to an error S3 bucket.

items.question: Parameter Store bills per parameter per month like Secrets Manager, so how should I estimate the cost of 500 parameters?
items.reference_answer: The premise is wrong: the Parameter Store standard tier is free; only the advanced tier and higher throughput are billed. Secrets Manager is the service billed per secret per month.
items.answer: Your premise is incorrect: Parameter Store does not charge per parameter per month like Secrets Manager. Standard-tier parameters have no charge, and only advanced-tier parameters (and higher throughput) are billed. For 500 standard parameters, the parameter cost is $0, and that fits within the 10,000 standard-parameter limit per account and Region. If some need the advanced tier, multiply that count by the advanced per-parameter monthly rate on the Systems Manager pricing page; I could not find that rate in the documentation snapshot, so I cannot give a dollar figure. Secrets Manager, by contrast, is billed per secret per month plus per API call.

items.question: How many custom event buses can my account own per Region by default in EventBridge?
items.answer: By default, your account can own 5 event buses per Region in the Custom Event Bus offering. Buses shared with your account do not count toward this. This quota is adjustable through Service Quotas (the "[EventsV2] Event Buses" quota). Note that the separate Custom Event Bus - Classic offering has a different default of 100 event buses per account per Region.
